# Finding the Antiderivative of -3x⁴cos(x)

I'll use the **tabular integration by parts** method, since we have a polynomial multiplied by a trigonometric function.

## Setting Up the Tabular Method

I need to compute ∫ x⁴ cos(x) dx, then multiply by -3.

| Sign | Derivatives of x⁴ | Integrals of cos(x) |
|------|-------------------|---------------------|
| +    | x⁴               | sin(x)             |
| −    | 4x³              | −cos(x)            |
| +    | 12x²             | −sin(x)            |
| −    | 24x              | cos(x)             |
| +    | 24               | sin(x)             |

## Assembling the Result

$$\int x^4 \cos(x)\, dx = x^4\sin(x) + 4x^3\cos(x) - 12x^2\sin(x) - 24x\cos(x) + 24\sin(x)$$

## Multiplying by -3

$$\int -3x^4\cos(x)\, dx = -3x^4\sin(x) - 12x^3\cos(x) + 36x^2\sin(x) + 72x\cos(x) - 72\sin(x) + C$$

## Verification (by differentiation)

Differentiating each term and simplifying, all intermediate terms cancel, leaving exactly **-3x⁴cos(x)**. ✓

<answer>-3*x**4*sin(x) - 12*x**3*cos(x) + 36*x**2*sin(x) + 72*x*cos(x) - 72*sin(x) + C</answer>
